Why it holds: adjacent chunks are similar; warm-starting from cached progress shrinks the denoising burden for the next horizon, keeping computation under the control-loop budget.

Why it holds: SIM(3)-equivariance (stronger than SO(2)) multiplies the reach of each demonstration by all scaled and rotated versions, so a 5-minute video covers a task class rather than a single setup.

Why it holds: discrete flow matching learns the forward process on a finite set; sampling in token space is fast and can represent multiple modes through different sequences; each sampled sequence is a complete multimodal plan that can be executed or refined.

The move: retrieve nearest-neighbor demonstrations, use their noise levels as a prior x_T ∼ N(μ_retr, σ_retr²), then run the reverse diffusion x_t = xt+Δt + σ²∇ log p(xt+Δt|c) from this tighter initialization. Why it holds: starting noise close to plausible solutions reduces the number of denoising steps needed and concentrates mass on high-confidence modes; retrieval grounds the prior in real demonstrations, so the reverse path stays in the support of the data distribution.

Gaussian-Mixture Latent Flow.work: Predicting 3D human motion for 'a person dancing' 1 second into the future has genuine multimodality: the dancer may spin left, spin right, or step forward. A unimodal baseline treats the motion as a single distribution and produces the averaging artifact—a slow mid-motion unrelated to any real dance. A GMM latent flow explicitly models ~4 modes in latent space. On a test set of 80 sequences, the average displacement error for the most-likely mode drops from ~0.45 m to ~0.28 m when compared mode-to-mode rather than averaging.
Gaussian-Mixture Latent Flow.math: The object is a Gaussian-mixture distribution p(yt:T|x) = Σ_k π_k N(y|μ_k(x), Σ_k) over diverse future 3D poses, learned in latent space. The move: apply flow matching in the latent code space zt+Δt = z_t + vφ(z_t,x)Δt, where vφ is trained to learn the gradient of the mixture log-density, then decode y = decoder(z). Why it holds: a Gaussian mixture in latent space represents multiple modes naturally; flow matching learns the velocity field that transports samples from noise toward the mixture components; this preserves multimodality and prevents mode collapse that averaging would cause.

PoseD-Flow.work: Completing a person's pose when the left arm is occluded requires reasoning about plausible arm configurations on SO(3), the 3D rotation group. Euclidean flow on joint angles can 'average' a full rotation with a straight arm into an invalid in-between pose. PoseD-Flow applies flow on the rotation manifold, respecting the geometry. PoseD-Flow.math: The object is a distribution over incomplete poses p(R|R_obs, c) where R ∈ SO(3)⊃J are the missing rotations (J joints) and R_obs are observed ones. The move: parameterize the flow on the rotation manifold using the tangent space exp(ξ̂): ξ̂ ∈ so(3) → R ∈ SO(3), then learn the geodesic velocity vφ(R,R_obs,c) that guides missing joints toward consistent poses. Why it holds: working on SO(3) preserves the manifold structure; the exponential map ensures sampled rotations are valid; geodesic flow respects the geometry of rotations, so occluded joints are completed in a way that respects the observed pose and scene.

RehearseVLA.work: A vision-language-action policy cloned from 4 human demonstrations can pick an object with ~55% success—only the grasp angles and object instances the human showed. A physically-consistent world model simulates rollouts and flags failures (collision, slip, missed grasp). Safe RL increases the probability of successful actions and decreases failing ones. After fine-tuning on imagined rollouts, success rate improves to ~82%, beating the expert's rate because the agent explores gripper widths the human never tried.
RehearseVLA.math: The object is a policy distribution π(a|o) after world-model feedback, represented as a vision-language-action model updated via reinforcement learning. Why it holds: world-model predictions provide safe RL feedback without environment interaction; the model makes errors, but feedback from constraints prevents unsafe actions from being learned; few demonstrations seed both the model and policy with plausible priors.

What it operates on: the current observation, the task condition, and a short sequence of future robot commands.

FDPP.work: A pretrained diffusion policy for 'pick and place' scores ~65% success on task variations it was trained on. A human rates pairwise videos: 'Trajectory A (smooth, slow) vs. Trajectory B (jerky, fast)'—A is preferred. FDPP learns a preference reward and fine-tunes the diffusion policy to maximize human-preferred trajectories. On a held-out set of 30 task instances, success rate climbs from ~65% to ~77%, and smoothness (jerk integral) improves 2.1× as well.
FDPP.math: The object is a reward function R∗(a|s) learned from pairwise human preferences, and a policy π(a|s) that maximizes the expected reward. The move: use the preference labels to train a reward classifier log&frac{exp Rφ(s,a+)}{ exp Rφ(s,a-) + exp Rφ(s,a+)} = preference, then fine-tune the diffusion policy via policy gradient π√ ← π + α ∇π E[R∗(a|s)]. Why it holds: the preference classifier learns a smooth reward surface from comparisons; policy gradient with this learned reward reshapes the generative distribution toward preferred actions; diffusion provides a flexible sampler that can be tilted by the reward without collapse.

What it operates on: the current observation, the task condition, and a short sequence of future robot commands.

Diffusion Meets DAgger.work: An eye-in-hand policy for 'pushing a block' is trained on 50 robot rollouts. The policy fails when the block ends up 5 cm away from the training distribution—DAgger asks the expert to label that state. Normally, generating new training states is expensive (robot time). Diffusion Meets DAgger uses a diffusion model trained on camera images to synthesize out-of-distribution block positions, then asks the expert to label the image (no robot needed). After 3 rounds of diffusion-augmented DAgger, the policy success rate on 20 new real states improves from ~54% to ~79%.
Diffusion Meets DAgger.math: The object is a policy π(a|o) and a data distribution p_data(s) over states encountered by the expert. The move: use diffusion to generate out-of-distribution states ŝ ∼ diffusion(s, noise, guidance), query an expert for the correct action a∗ ∼ π_expert(ŝ), and add (ŝ, a∗) to the training set; then fine-tune the learned policy. Why it holds: diffusion generates plausible OOD states that interpolate between observed contexts; labeling these states with expert actions covers the gaps in the cloned policy; iterating this process is DAgger, and diffusion ensures OOD states are realistic so the expert labels are correct.

What it operates on: the current observation, the task condition, and a short sequence of future robot commands.

The operation: define a policy distribution after feedback; train a denoiser, flow, or guided sampler on demonstrations or feedback; then sample a coherent action chunk and execute only the first part before replanning.

Chain-of-Imagination.work: A robot tasked with 'fetch the mug from the kitchen and place it on the desk' needs to break this into sub-goals: 'go to kitchen', 'find and grasp mug', 'navigate to desk', 'place mug'. Directly optimizing a raw diffusion policy over 50+ timesteps is hard. Chain-of-Imagination uses an MLLM to output intermediate visual goals (e.g., a diffusion-rendered image of 'gripper holding mug at desk'), and the diffusion policy acts toward each sub-goal. Success rate on 10 long-horizon tasks improves from ~35% (end-to-end) to ~68% with intermediate visual guidance.
Chain-of-Imagination.math: The object is a trajectory s_0 → s₂_1 → ... → s_T where intermediate states s₂_i are visual sub-goals generated by an MLLM. The move: sample a subgoal sequence with the MLLM s₂ ∼ MLLM(s_0, c), use diffusion to interpolate or refine each segment ŝt:i ∼ diffusion(s_t, s₂_i, c_segment), then execute actions a_t ∼ π(a|s_t, s₂_i) toward each sub-goal. Why it holds: the MLLM generates plausible sub-goals aligned with language; diffusion ensures smooth, feasible transitions between them; hierarchical action—first imagining, then doing—reduces the burden on the low-level policy and improves credit assignment.

EquivariantDiffusionPolicy.work: A robot must grasp mugs at every possible angle. Collect 50 demonstrations: grasp at 0°, 30°, 60°, …, 330°. A naive network sees 50 independent examples. Train with SO(2) equivariance: the network is built so that rotating the input scene also rotates the output action. Now one demo at 0° automatically teaches the network to grasp at every angle. Effective training set: 50 × (360/30) = 600 equivalent rotations. On the same 50 physical demos, equivariant policies achieve the stated 21.9% improvement in success.
